messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Alejandro's eyes still scanned the crowded streets of Manhattan with a mix of unease and instinctual vigilance. It had been two years since his deployment to Afghanistan ended, but the memories of that fateful day lingered, refusing to be shaken off. The IED blast that killed three of his comrades was forever seared into his mind – every explosion of a car horn or revving engine triggered an immediate flashback. He would see the mangled wreckage, smell the acrid smoke, and hear the anguished cries of his friends. These vivid memories were not just painful; they also made Alejandro feel like he had no future, that everything was doomed from the start. As a financial analyst, Alejandro spent most of his days staring at spreadsheets, trying to make sense of numbers that seemed meaningless compared to the chaos he experienced during combat. But even in this sterile environment, fragments of memories would suddenly appear – a glimpse of a mangled leg, the sound of gunfire – and then vanish just as quickly. These sudden pieces made it impossible for him to piece together what really happened that day; his recollections were disjointed and unclear, leaving him with more questions than answers. What haunted Alejandro most was not just the loss he suffered but also the actions he took in its aftermath – the desperation, the fear, the anger that consumed him. He became convinced that he had acted in ways that went against who he truly was, that some fundamental part of himself had been shattered beyond repair. Alejandro's inability to reconcile his past and present selves led him to withdraw from social interactions. He stopped attending gatherings or parties, fearing that someone might ask about his experiences during the war. Talking about it would only bring up more painful memories, which he struggled to keep at bay even on good days. Open spaces also made him uneasy; he felt exposed, vulnerable, and easily targeted – as if the skyscrapers towering above him were potential snipers' nests. Avoiding these triggers became his primary coping mechanism, a way to maintain some semblance of control over his emotions. However, this avoidance only strengthened Alejandro's negative appraisals of himself. By not confronting his fears or memories head-on, he reinforced the notion that he was hopeless and forever changed – an outsider looking in at a world that seemed whole and unscathed while he felt broken and fragmented. His memories continued to torment him, each recollection fueling the cycle of self-doubt and despair. Lately, Alejandro has been waking up to nightmares more frequently, reliving the same traumatic scenes with eerie vividness. The cumulative effect is starting to seep into his daily life; he's begun to struggle at work, unable to concentrate on tasks that once came easily. It was this creeping sense of dysfunction – and a dawning realization that avoidance wasn't working – that finally brought Alejandro to seek help. He hopes that by confronting the very memories he's tried so hard to suppress, he might slowly rebuild a future worth living in, one where his past no longer defines him as an outsider forever trapped in a cycle of pain.
